raw_case_text:
A 19-year-old previously healthy Japanese woman was admitted to our hospital with an alveolar hemorrhage, deep vein thrombosis (DVT), and pulmonary embolism (PE) in January 2013. One month before admission, she developed a dry cough, followed by hemosputum, fever, and right-sided chest pain. She was suspected of having pneumonia on the basis of a chest X-ray and was administered antibiotics. However, her symptoms gradually worsened and she was referred to a department of respiratory disease at another hospital. Bronchoscopy revealed alveolar hemorrhage and computed tomography (CT) scans showed DVT and PE. Since she also had additional abnormal findings, such as prolonged dilute Russell viper venom time (dRVVT) and was positive for antinuclear antibodies (ANA, 1 : 320) (Table 1), she was suspected of having SLE-related APS and then transferred to our hospital.
On admission, physical examination showed decreased breathing sounds in her right back on auscultation and her left leg was swollen and painful. Her body temperature was 37.3 C, and she had a blood pressure of 104/62 mmHg. She had a regular heart rate of 92/min and a respiratory rate of 31/min with oxygen saturation of 98% in room air. Laboratory studies on admission revealed a white blood count of 10,220/muL, hemoglobin level of 11.8 g/dL, and platelet count of 287 x 103/muL. The C-reactive protein level was 10.3 mg/dL. Liver function tests were normal. An electrocardiogram and echocardiogram did not reveal any abnormalities. Coagulation tests revealed normal prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, and fibrinogen, but a marked elevation of both FDP and D-dimer levels (113 mug/mL and 46.8 mug/mL, resp.). Chest radiography revealed consolidations in the bilateral lower lungs and a right pleural effusion. An enhanced CT scan showed a PE in the right pulmonary artery with bilateral consolidation in the lungs as well as extensive DVT throughout the inferior vena cava (IVC) to the left posterior tibial vein (Figure 1). A ventilation-perfusion scintigraphy confirmed multiple areas of mismatch compatible with a PE in both lungs (Figure 2(a)). She had no past or family history of thrombosis. Based on previous clinical symptoms and laboratory data, she was suspected to have (SLE-related) APS complicated with alveolar hemorrhage at the time of admission. She was treated with intravenous methylprednisolone pulse therapy (1 g/day for 3 days) followed by 1 mg/kg of oral prednisolone (PSL) in combination with oral tacrolimus (TAC) administration (3 mg/day). The day after admission, she had an IVC filter implanted and was given anticoagulation therapy with heparin and, a few days later, warfarin.
Compared with the previous results, her immunological tests in our hospital were negative for ANA and showed normal titers of aPL, including LAC (dRVVT), IgM aCL, and anti-beta2 glycoprotein I (beta2GPI) antibodies (Table 1). Other autoimmune markers for SLE were negative. To further explore thrombocytopenia, serological viral tests were performed. The results were positive for CMV-IgM and CMV-IgG and negative for hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) viral capsid antigen IgM, EBV early antigen IgG, and parvovirus B19 IgM. To confirm whether or not it was an acute CMV infection, a PCR test for CMV (geni-Q) was performed using serum sample obtained on admission, and the tests revealed a positive result (200 copy/muL). No pathological values for plasma anti-thrombin III, protein C, and S activity were found.
Taken together, she was thought to have developed DVT/PE and alveolar hemorrhage due to the transient appearance of aPL, that is, LAC, associated with acute CMV infection. Therefore, the PSL was tapered rapidly and TAC was stopped thereafter. The platelet count as well as the fibrinogen degradation product (FDP) and D-dimer values gradually returned to normal levels within three weeks. At the time of discharge, an antigenemia assay for CMV pp65 (C7-HRP) was negative. Seven months later, she was completely asymptomatic and her IVC filter was removed. Her CMV-IgM titer decreased with an elevation of her CMV-IgG titer (Table 2). Ten months later, a follow-up ventilation-perfusion scintigraphy (Figure 2(b)) and CT scan confirmed significant resolution of the previous PE and DVT. Finally, after one year, PSL and anticoagulant therapy were stopped, and she has been well without recurrence to date.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 19-year-old previously healthy Japanese woman presented in January 2013 with a 1-month history of dry cough progressing to hemoptysis, fever, right-sided chest pain, and painful left lower-extremity swelling.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: One month prior to admission, the patient developed a dry cough followed by hemosputum, fever, and right-sided pleuritic chest pain unresponsive to outpatient antibiotics for presumed pneumonia. Evaluation at a referring hospital revealed alveolar hemorrhage on bronchoscopy, deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE) on CT, prolonged dilute Russell viper venom time (dRVVT), and positive ANA (1:320), prompting transfer to our hospital for suspected SLE-related antiphospholipid syndrome.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy; no personal or family history of thrombosis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for dry cough, hemosputum/hemoptysis, fever, right-sided chest pain, and painful left leg swelling.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature 37.3 °C, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, heart rate 92/min, respiratory rate 31/min, SpO2 98% on room air; decreased breath sounds over the right posterior lung field; swollen and tender left lower extremity.
objective.routine_investigations: Referring hospital labs: prolonged dRVVT and positive ANA (1:320). Admission labs at our hospital: WBC 10,220/uL, hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL, platelets 287 x 10^3/uL (subsequent transient thrombocytopenia), CRP 10.3 mg/dL, normal LFTs, normal PT, aPTT, fibrinogen, antithrombin III, protein C, and protein S activities, and markedly elevated fibrin degradation products (FDP 113 ug/mL) and D-dimer (46.8 ug/mL). Repeat autoimmune panel at our hospital was negative for ANA, lupus anticoagulant (dRVVT), IgM anticardiolipin, anti-beta2-glycoprotein I antibodies, and other SLE markers. Viral serologies were positive for CMV IgM and CMV IgG and negative for HBsAg, HCV, EBV VCA-IgM, EBV EA-IgG, and parvovirus B19 IgM (discharge CMV pp65 antigenemia C7-HRP was negative; 7-month follow-up showed decreased CMV IgM and elevated CMV IgG). Chest X-ray showed bilateral lower lung consolidations and right pleural effusion; ECG and echocardiogram were normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Referring hospital bronchoscopy confirmed alveolar hemorrhage. Contrast-enhanced chest and venous CT demonstrated a right pulmonary artery embolism, bilateral lower lobe pulmonary consolidations, and extensive deep vein thrombosis extending from the inferior vena cava (IVC) to the left posterior tibial vein; ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) lung scintigraphy confirmed multiple bilateral perfusion mismatches. Quantitative serum CMV PCR (geni-Q) on admission serum was positive at 200 copies/uL.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Diagnosed with extensive inferior vena cava/left lower extremity deep vein thrombosis, bilateral pulmonary embolism, and diffuse alveolar hemorrhage secondary to transient antiphospholipid/lupus anticoagulant antibodies triggered by acute primary cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection in an immunocompetent young woman (confirmed by positive CMV IgM and IgG, admission serum CMV PCR of 200 copies/uL, and subsequent seroconversion with normalization of transient ANA and dRVVT). Initially treated for presumed SLE-APS with pulse IV methylprednisolone (1 g/day for 3 days) followed by oral prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day), oral tacrolimus (3 mg/day), IVC filter placement, and unfractionated heparin bridged to warfarin. Once acute CMV-induced transient APS was confirmed, tacrolimus was discontinued and prednisolone rapidly tapered; FDP, D-dimer, and platelets normalized within 3 weeks, the IVC filter was removed at 7 months, V/Q scan and CT confirmed thrombus resolution at 10 months, and anticoagulation and steroids were stopped at 1 year without recurrence.
